cv_tip_1_message: Unless you have 10+ years of experience, one page is enough. Recruiters scan a CV in seconds.
cv_tip_2_message: Replace "handled sales" with "increased monthly sales by 25%". Numbers make your impact believable.
cv_tip_3_message: Reuse the exact keywords and skills from the job post so ATS filters and recruiters see the match.
cv_tip_4_message: State your title, years of experience and strongest value. Tailor it to the role you're applying for.
cv_tip_5_message: Something like firstname.lastname@gmail.com. Avoid nicknames or random numbers.
cv_tip_6_message: Led, Built, Reduced, Launched, Improved. Strong verbs make every line sound active.
cv_tip_7_message: Separate technical skills from soft skills and list the ones most relevant to the job first.
cv_tip_8_message: Use one font family, size 10–12 pt, with clear headings. Readability beats decoration.
cv_tip_9_message: Typos are one of the fastest ways to get rejected. Read it twice, then let someone else read it.
cv_tip_10_message: List your latest experience first. It's the format recruiters and ATS expect.
cv_tip_11_message: Don't just list what you were responsible for; explain what changed because of your work.
cv_tip_12_message: "Experience", "Education", "Skills". Creative titles can confuse ATS software.
cv_tip_13_message: Degree, school and year are enough. Add GPA or courses only if you're a fresh graduate.
cv_tip_14_message: Make sure the profile is up to date and matches your CV. Use a clean custom URL.
cv_tip_15_message: Projects prove skills when experience is limited. Include a link to the work if you can.
cv_tip_16_message: Write in short, impersonal phrases. Bullets are much easier to scan than paragraphs.
cv_tip_17_message: Under each job, place the achievement most relevant to the target role at the top.
cv_tip_18_message: 8–12 well-chosen skills beat 30 generic ones. Only list what you can discuss in an interview.
cv_tip_19_message: Everything on your CV can be checked. Exaggerations often surface during interviews.
cv_tip_20_message: PDF keeps your layout intact. Name it clearly, e.g. Name_JobTitle_CV.pdf.
cv_tip_21_title: Open your summary with your title
cv_tip_21_message: Start with who you are (e.g. "Flutter developer with 3 years of experience"), then your key strength.
cv_tip_22_message: Avoid tables, text boxes, images and multiple columns; many ATS systems can't read them.
cv_tip_23_message: Pick one style (e.g. Jan 2023 – Mar 2025) and use it everywhere.
cv_tip_24_message: Enough to show impact, short enough to stay readable. Use fewer bullets for older jobs.
cv_tip_25_title: Keep each bullet under two lines
cv_tip_25_message: If a bullet needs three lines, split it or cut the detail that doesn't prove impact.
cv_tip_26_message: Phone with country code, email, and city. A full home address isn't necessary.
cv_tip_27_message: Name the tools, software or methods you used in each role. They double as keywords.
cv_tip_28_message: Include name, issuer and year. Skip old or unrelated certificates.
cv_tip_29_message: Say what problem you solved, what you did, and what came out of it.
cv_tip_30_message: "Hard-working" and "team player" say nothing. Prove them with a concrete example instead.
cv_tip_31_title: Match top skills to the role
cv_tip_31_message: Put the 5 skills the job asks for most at the top of your skills section.
cv_tip_32_message: Write "Search Engine Optimization (SEO)" the first time so both humans and ATS catch it.
cv_tip_33_message: Internships, volunteering, university projects and freelance work all count.
cv_tip_34_message: The upper third of page one is read the most. Put your title, summary and best highlights there.
cv_tip_35_message: Past tense for previous jobs, present tense for your current role.
cv_tip_36_message: Skip marital status, ID numbers and unrelated hobbies. Space is precious.
cv_tip_37_message: Margins around 2 cm and spacing between sections make the CV easier on the eyes.
cv_tip_38_message: Promotions, growing responsibility and new titles at the same company tell a strong story.
cv_tip_39_message: Roles older than 10–15 years or unrelated to the target job can be shortened or removed.
cv_tip_40_message: Awkward phrasing and repetition are easy to hear. Then have a friend review it.
cv_tip_41_message: A gap longer than 6 months is better explained than hidden. Add a short line like “Career break – full-time course in data analysis.”
cv_tip_42_message: Finish the rest of the CV first, then pull your best 2–3 facts into the summary. It will be sharper and consistent with what you actually wrote.
cv_tip_43_message: When you have an outcome, start the bullet with it: “Cut onboarding time 30% by redesigning the checklist.” The number is what gets remembered.
cv_tip_44_message: “Python” says little. “Python — 3 years, data pipelines and automation” proves it. Add level or context to your top 5 skills.
cv_tip_45_message: A scanned or photographed CV is just an image, so screening software reads nothing. Export a text-based PDF from your editor instead.
cv_tip_46_title: Fresh grad? Show your capstone result
cv_tip_46_message: Give your thesis or graduation project one line with its outcome: “Inventory app used by 40 students.” It proves skills a bare degree can’t.
cv_tip_47_message: Open each link in a private window and check that it works from your PDF. A dead or private link hurts more than no link at all.
cv_tip_48_message: City and country are enough, no full address. Add one line on relocation, remote work, or notice period so recruiters can shortlist you quickly.
cv_tip_49_message: Delete “responsible for”, “worked on”, and “helped with”. Replace them with the action itself: “Managed…”, “Built…”, “Reduced…”.
cv_tip_50_message: Bold only job titles, companies, and your key numbers. When everything is bold, nothing stands out.
cv_tip_51_message: It is assumed and wastes a line. Keep a reference list ready to share when someone actually asks for it.
cv_tip_52_message: Skip “Job seeker.” Use role + specialty + value: “Data Analyst | SQL & Power BI | Turning sales data into decisions.”
cv_tip_53_message: Studying now? Add “Data Analytics Certificate — in progress, completes in 2 months.” It shows momentum and closes skill gaps honestly.
cv_tip_54_title: State your exact role in team projects
cv_tip_54_message: Write what you personally did: “Built the payment module in a team of 4.” Interviewers will ask, so keep it clear and true.
cv_tip_55_title: Add a photo only if the market expects it
cv_tip_55_message: Photos are common in some regions and discouraged in others. If you add one, use a clear, well-lit headshot with a plain background.
cv_tip_56_message: If five bullets start with “Managed”, rotate: led, launched, streamlined, negotiated, trained. Precise verbs also show what you really did.
cv_tip_57_message: Choose one restrained accent color for headings and check that the CV still reads clearly when printed in black and white.
cv_tip_58_title: Keep Arabic and English versions consistent
cv_tip_58_message: Don’t machine-translate. Write each version properly, and make sure titles, dates, and numbers match exactly across both.
cv_tip_59_title: Put your CV keywords on LinkedIn
cv_tip_59_message: Recruiters search by keyword. Repeat your key skills in About, Experience, and Skills so you appear in their results.
cv_tip_60_title: Put your target title under your name
cv_tip_60_message: A one-line headline like “Senior Accountant | IFRS | Cairo” tells the reader who you are before they read a single line of the body.
cv_tip_61_message: Replace “seeking a challenging opportunity” with the exact job title and industry you are targeting. Vague summaries get skipped; specific ones get matched.
cv_tip_62_title: Show the scale of your work
cv_tip_62_message: Add size to major bullets: team of 6, 200 clients, $50K budget, 15K monthly users. Scale tells a recruiter your level faster than a job title.
cv_tip_63_message: Skip “Microsoft Word”, “internet”, or “typing” unless the job asks for them. Basic skills waste space your stronger skills deserve.
cv_tip_64_message: Paste your CV into a plain text editor. If the order breaks or characters vanish, screening software will struggle too. Fix the layout until it reads cleanly.
cv_tip_65_title: Search for the last company’s name
cv_tip_65_message: Before sending, search your CV and email for the previous company’s name. Leaving the wrong one in is a classic mistake that gets noticed instantly.
cv_tip_66_message: Ask a manager or client to recommend one specific strength, and gather endorsements for your top skills. Social proof builds trust before the first call.
cv_tip_67_title: Open with a selected achievements block
cv_tip_67_message: With 5+ years of experience, place your 3 biggest wins in a short block above your job history so busy readers see your best proof first.
cv_tip_68_message: Changing fields? Open with a sentence linking past strengths to the new role: “Teacher turned UX researcher: 8 years explaining complex ideas to diverse users.”
cv_tip_69_message: Without metrics, use frequency, volume, speed, or rank: “handled 40+ tickets daily”, “top 3 of 20 performers”, “delivered ahead of deadline.”
cv_tip_70_title: Drop tools you haven’t touched in years
cv_tip_70_message: A tool you last used 6+ years ago can signal outdated skills. Remove it or mark it “familiar” so your list reads current.
cv_tip_71_title: Keep key info out of headers and footers
cv_tip_71_message: Some screening software ignores headers and footers. Put your name, email, and phone in the main body of the page.
cv_tip_72_message: Say what the award means: “Top 5% of 300 students” or “Won national hackathon, 60 teams.” A bare title tells the reader nothing.
cv_tip_73_title: Use a project to fill a skill gap
cv_tip_73_message: Missing experience with a required tool? Build a small project with it and list it. It shows initiative and gives you something concrete to discuss.
cv_tip_74_title: Use one spelling of your name everywhere
cv_tip_74_message: Arabic names have several English spellings. Pick one and use it on your CV, LinkedIn, and email so recruiters can find and match you.
cv_tip_75_message: Digits and symbols catch the eye: “40%”, “7 years”, “$2M.” Spelled-out numbers blend into the sentence.
cv_tip_76_title: Check it on a phone screen
cv_tip_76_message: Many recruiters open CVs on their phones. View your PDF on one: if the text is tiny or lines wrap oddly, simplify the layout.
cv_tip_77_title: Write tool names the standard way
cv_tip_77_message: JavaScript, GitHub, PostgreSQL, not “Java script” or “Github”. Exact spellings match what recruiters type into search.
cv_tip_78_title: Use plain bullets, skip emoji and icons
cv_tip_78_message: Stick to standard round bullets. Emoji, arrows, and icon fonts can turn into garbled boxes when software reads your file.
cv_tip_79_message: Didn’t finish? Write “BSc Computer Science, 3 years completed” or your expected graduation date. It’s honest and still shows your training.
cv_tip_80_message: Users, downloads, GitHub stars, or revenue turn a side project into evidence: “Budget app, 2,000 downloads, 4.6★.”
cv_tip_81_title: Mention WhatsApp if your market uses it
cv_tip_81_message: In many regions recruiters reach out on WhatsApp. If yours does, note that your number has it, and keep your profile photo professional.
cv_tip_82_message: Project codenames and internal acronyms mean nothing outside your company. Say what it is: “internal CRM” instead of “Project Falcon.”
cv_tip_83_title: Align everything to one left edge
cv_tip_83_message: Headings, dates, and bullets that line up on a consistent grid look deliberate. Random indents look like a template gone wrong.
cv_tip_84_message: Recruiters often search your name. Check the first results and tighten privacy or clean up public posts that don’t fit the job you want.
cv_tip_85_title: Turn on Open to Work for recruiters only
cv_tip_85_message: Choose the recruiters-only option so your current employer doesn’t see it, and list 2–3 target job titles.
cv_tip_86_message: If a job stresses certifications or projects, move that section up. Section order is a free way to tailor your CV without rewriting it.
cv_tip_87_title: Put key tools in the summary
cv_tip_87_message: Mention your 2–3 most relevant tools or skills in the summary itself. Both software filters and busy readers catch them there first.
cv_tip_88_message: Employers pay for four things: more money, lower cost, saved time, or reduced risk. Check that every key bullet points to at least one.
cv_tip_89_message: After your first draft, cut 20% of the words. What survives is usually the strongest, and your CV gets easier to skim.
cv_tip_90_title: Match the paper size to the market
cv_tip_90_message: Use A4 for most of the world and US Letter for the US and Canada. The wrong size can shift your layout when someone prints it.
cv_tip_91_message: Reasons for leaving, salary history, and complaints about past bosses don’t belong on a CV. Save any explanation for the interview.
cv_tip_92_message: Pin your best project, article, or CV highlights to Featured. It’s the first proof a visitor sees below your headline.
cv_tip_93_message: If you need a second page, fill at least a third of it and don’t split a job entry across the break. Three orphan lines look like an accident.
cv_tip_94_title: State your industry, not just your role
cv_tip_94_message: “Marketing specialist” is generic; “Marketing specialist in fintech and e-commerce” matches searches and shows you already know the field.
cv_tip_95_message: If the company or title isn’t well known, add context: “Fintech startup, 200 staff” or “Associate (Frontend Developer).” It saves the reader a search.
cv_tip_96_title: Rate languages on a standard scale
cv_tip_96_message: “Good English” is vague. Use CEFR levels (B2, C1) or a test score like IELTS 7.0 so employers can compare you.
cv_tip_97_message: Progress bars and star ratings are just images to software and mean little to humans. Write “Advanced” or years of use instead.
cv_tip_98_message: Applying abroad? Add the scale next to your grade: “Very Good (3.2/4.0 equivalent).” Foreign recruiters can’t judge a grade they can’t place.
cv_tip_99_title: Link a case study, not a folder
cv_tip_99_message: Designers, writers, and marketers: link one short page explaining the goal, your process, and the result, not a dump of files.
cv_tip_100_title: Write a clear email subject line
cv_tip_100_message: When emailing your CV, use “Application – Job Title – Your Name.” It’s easy to file and shows you follow instructions.
cv_gap_email_message: Recruiters need a way to reach you. Add a professional email to your CV.
cv_gap_phone_message: Include a number with country code so employers can call you quickly.
cv_gap_summary_message: A 2–3 line summary at the top helps recruiters understand you fast.
cv_gap_experience_message: Add jobs, internships or freelance work, even short ones.
cv_gap_achievements_message: Your experience has no measurable results. Add figures like percentages, counts or amounts.
cv_gap_skills_message: List at least 5 skills relevant to the jobs you're targeting.
cv_gap_education_message: Add your degree, school and graduation year.
cv_gap_link_title: Add a LinkedIn or portfolio link
cv_gap_link_message: A profile link gives employers more proof of your work.
cv_gap_projects_message: Projects show your skills when your experience is limited.
cv_gap_languages_message: List the languages you speak and your level in each.
